mcqs.question: In science, how is the term 'colour' of a material defined?

options.A: The way a material feels when touched.
options.B: The visual sensation produced when a material reflects or absorbs certain wavelengths of light.
options.C: The temperature a material reaches when heated.
options.D: The hardness of a material measured by scratching.

mcqs.answer: The visual sensation produced when a material reflects or absorbs certain wavelengths of light.
mcqs.explanation: Colour is the visual sensation we see because a material reflects some wavelengths of visible light and absorbs others. It is not related to touch, temperature, or hardness, which are different observable properties.

mcqs.question: Which of the following materials would be best chosen for a shiny decorative object because it has a high lustre?
mcqs.explanation: Metals have free electrons that reflect most of the incident light, giving them a bright, shiny appearance (high lustre). Wood, plastic, and cotton are generally dull and do not reflect light as strongly.

mcqs.question: Which example best illustrates the texture property of a material?

options.A: A piece of glass that lets light pass through.
options.B: A sheet of sandpaper that feels rough when touched.
options.C: A bottle of water that is clear.
options.D: A block of oil that is slippery.

mcqs.answer: A sheet of sandpaper that feels rough when touched.
mcqs.explanation: Texture refers to how a surface feels to the touch. Sandpaper is characteristically rough, making it a clear example of texture. The other options describe transparency or slipperiness, not texture.

mcqs.learning_point: Using observable properties to group materials
mcqs.question: A teacher asks students to sort the following items into groups based on observable properties such as colour and texture: (i) a red smooth marble, (ii) a blue rough stone, (iii) a green smooth plastic bottle, (iv) a yellow rough wooden block. Which grouping is most appropriate?

options.A: Group 1 – red marble and green plastic bottle; Group 2 – blue stone and yellow wooden block.
options.B: Group 1 – smooth items (red marble, green plastic bottle); Group 2 – rough items (blue stone, yellow wooden block).
options.C: Group 1 – red and blue items; Group 2 – green and yellow items.
options.D: Group 1 – marble and stone; Group 2 – plastic bottle and wooden block.

mcqs.answer: Group 1 – smooth items (red marble, green plastic bottle); Group 2 – rough items (blue stone, yellow wooden block).
mcqs.explanation: Sorting by observable properties means using characteristics we can see or feel. Grouping by texture (smooth vs rough) correctly separates the items, while the other options mix different properties or ignore texture altogether.

mcqs.question: Which statement about colour is a common misconception?

options.A: Colour depends on the wavelengths of light a material reflects.
options.B: All red objects are made of the same material.
options.C: A material can appear different colours under different lighting.
options.D: Colour can be used as one of the observable properties to classify materials.

mcqs.answer: All red objects are made of the same material.
mcqs.explanation: The colour of an object is determined by the light it reflects, not by its chemical composition. Different materials (e.g., red cloth, red plastic, red metal) can all appear red, so the idea that all red objects are the same material is a misconception.

mcqs.question: Why do metals usually have a bright, shiny appearance (high lustre)?

options.A: Because their surface is always smooth.
options.B: Because free electrons on the surface reflect most of the incident light.
options.C: Because they absorb all colours of light.

mcqs.answer: Because free electrons on the surface reflect most of the incident light.
mcqs.explanation: Metals contain free electrons that can move easily. When light hits a metal surface, these electrons reflect most of the light, giving metals their characteristic shiny (high‑lustre) appearance. Smoothness or polishing can enhance lustre but is not the fundamental reason.

mcqs.question: Match each material with its typical texture. Which pair is correctly matched?
mcqs.explanation: Glass has a smooth surface that feels even to the touch. Sandpaper is rough, silk is smooth, and tree bark is generally rough, making options A, B, and D incorrect.

mcqs.learning_point: Using observable properties to group materials
mcqs.question: In a competitive exam, students are asked to group the following materials based on observable properties (colour, texture, and lustre): (i) a shiny silver metal spoon, (ii) a dull brown wooden stick, (iii) a smooth transparent glass window, (iv) a rough grey stone. Which grouping correctly uses observable properties?

options.A: Group 1 – shiny metal spoon and smooth glass window; Group 2 – dull wooden stick and rough stone.
options.B: Group 1 – shiny metal spoon and dull wooden stick; Group 2 – smooth glass window and rough stone.
options.C: Group 1 – smooth glass window and rough stone; Group 2 – shiny metal spoon and dull wooden stick.
options.D: Group 1 – shiny metal spoon alone; Group 2 – the other three together.

mcqs.answer: Group 1 – shiny metal spoon and smooth glass window; Group 2 – dull wooden stick and rough stone.
mcqs.explanation: Group 1 contains items that are smooth and have a high lustre (the metal spoon is shiny and the glass window is smooth and reflects light). Group 2 contains items with low lustre and a rough texture (the wooden stick is dull and the stone is rough). This grouping uses the observable properties consistently, whereas the other options mix unrelated properties.
